title: The Trade Desk Reports Q2 After the Close — Here's the Setup
subtitle: Advertiser budgets are tight and the stock has been crushed, but the bull case is built on CTV growth, AI-driven margins, and a valuation that's rarely been cheaper.
summary: The Trade Desk reports Q2 results after the close, testing whether its guided $750 million floor and 40 percent full-year margin target can survive another round of advertiser caution.

bodyHtml:
Tonight, after the closing bell, The Trade Desk tells investors whether the worst advertising stretch of its public life is easing or just taking a breather. The Q2 report lands after the close, with the call at 5 p.m. ET, and the setup could hardly be more loaded: a stock that has been crushed, a management team that guided conservatively in May, and a bull case that rests on what happens next, not what already happened. A company that spent most of its life at 20 to 30 times forward earnings now changes hands at roughly 10 times — a bargain only if the growth engine is still intact. That is the question tonight.

The last quarter explains the skepticism. In May, The Trade Desk reported Q1 revenue of $689 million, up 12 percent year over year, with non-GAAP EPS of $0.28 and adjusted EBITDA of $206 million, a 30 percent margin. Solid numbers — but the guidance was the story. Management guided Q2 revenue to at least $750 million, a bar set below the roughly $771 million the Street had been modeling. The stock got punished, and the message was plain: advertisers are being careful with budgets amid tariffs, geopolitical noise, and softness in consumer categories like CPG and autos. The Trade Desk is a demand-side platform — when marketers trim, it feels it first.

Step back, though, and the underlying business is in decent shape. Trailing-twelve-month revenue sits around $3 billion. Free cash flow ran to roughly $830 million over that period, up 20 percent year over year in Q1 alone, and the balance sheet is essentially pristine: about $1.4 billion in cash against $424 million in debt that is mostly capital leases — net cash near $1 billion. No dilution, no refinancing risk, no wall of maturities. This is a company that can afford to be patient while the ad cycle works itself out — more than you can say for most names at a decade-low multiple.

The bull case rests on three pillars, and none of them depend on this quarter being spectacular. First, connected TV — the fastest-growing major ad channel and the one place The Trade Desk genuinely competes with the walled gardens of Google, Amazon, Meta, and Netflix on the open internet. Second, Kokai, the AI decisioning engine replacing its legacy platform — a step change in how campaigns are planned and optimized, and the vehicle for the margin story. Third, the margins: the company still targets a 40 percent or better adjusted EBITDA margin for the full year, maintained even after the soft Q2 guide. If The Trade Desk can grow double digits and push margins toward 40 percent, the math at 10 times forward earnings gets interesting fast.

Add one more tell: Jeff Green, the founder and CEO, bought roughly $150 million of stock near the lows. Founders do not usually put that kind of money to work when they think the story is broken. Analysts remain cautious — consensus is Hold with a mean price target around $24 — but the range of targets, $11 to $38, is the market admitting it has no idea how this resolves.

So what matters tonight? First, the headline: revenue at or above the $750 million floor against consensus around $751.6 million, with EPS in the $0.40 to $0.41 range. Beating the floor is not the same as beating old expectations — the Street has already walked its numbers down. Second, Q3 guidance. That is where the real signal lives, because it tells you whether advertiser caution is fading or hardening. Third, the margin trajectory: whether management re-affirms that 40 percent full-year target, and how much of it is Kokai-driven efficiency versus plain austerity. Fourth, anything concrete on CTV momentum and UID2 identity adoption — the areas where The Trade Desk's differentiation shows up in the numbers. Fifth, listen for tone on the macro: tariffs, budgets, and the CPG and auto categories that have been the weak spots.

The honest read: this is a high-quality business in a soft patch, priced like the soft patch is permanent. The Trade Desk does not need a blowout tonight. It needs to prove the floor holds, the margin target survives contact, and the recovery narrative has somewhere to go. If it delivers that, a stock down roughly half year to date and about 80 percent below its high has room to re-rate. If it does not, the 10-times multiple starts to look less like a bargain and more like fair value. Either way, you will know by the time the call wraps up.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in TTD. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
